
# Packages and Datasets
***

The book works from a small number of datasets on purpose, so that by the time you reach multiple regression the variables are familiar and only the method is new.
The main running example is `Wages1`, and `USArrests` appears mostly in Test Yourself callouts and exercises.
This appendix lists each dataset, what its variables mean, and which chapters use it, followed by every package the book uses.

## Datasets

| Dataset | Source | Observations | Chapters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `USArrests` | built in | 50 US states in 1973 | 2--3, 5--8, 10--17, 19--24, 29 |
| `state.region` | built in | 50 US states in 1977 | 3, 12--14, 21, 23, 29 |
| `anscombe` | built in | 11 points in each of four pairs, published in 1973 | 15 |
| `UCBAdmissions` | built in | 24 cells of Berkeley graduate admissions in 1973 | 14, 21 |
| `LifeCycleSavings` | built in | 50 countries, averaged over 1960--1970 | 3, 21 |
| `Wages1` | `Ecdat` package | 3294 workers in 1987 | 2--3, 5--8, 10--25, 29 |
| `wage2` | `wooldridge` package | 935 US working men in 1980 | 13, 29 |
| `finance-charts-apple.csv` | web | 506 trading days from 2015--2017 | 26 |
| `tylervigen.csv` | web | varies, yearly within 1996--2010 | 28 |

The help page `?Ecdat::Wages1` says 1976--1982, but those dates belong to `Ecdat::Wages`; [the publisher's note on the source data](https://www.wiley.com/legacy/wileychi/verbeek2ed/datasets.html) says 1987.

Built-in datasets need no download: type the name to see the data, and `?USArrests` for the help page.
The others load as follows.
The two CSV files need an internet connection and could change or move, which is itself a reproducibility lesson.

```r
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat') # after install.packages('Ecdat')
data(wage2, package='wooldridge') # after install.packages('wooldridge')
stock <- read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/finance-charts-apple.csv')
vigen_csv <- read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-mad-statter/whysospurious/master/data-raw/tylervigen.csv')
```

## Variables

| Dataset | Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `USArrests` | `Murder`, `Assault`, `Rape` | Arrests per 100,000 residents |
| | `UrbanPop` | Percent of the state population living in urban areas |
| `state.region` | (a factor) | Census region: Northeast, South, North Central, or West |
| `anscombe` | `x1`--`x4`, `y1`--`y4` | Four $x$, $y$ pairs with nearly identical means, variances, correlations, and regression lines, but very different scatterplots |
| `UCBAdmissions` | `Admit`, `Gender`, `Dept` | Admission outcome (2), gender (2), and department (6), for $2\times2\times6=24$ cells |
| `LifeCycleSavings` | `sr` | Aggregate personal savings as a percent of disposable income |
| | `pop15`, `pop75` | Percent of the population under age 15, and over age 75 |
| | `dpi`, `ddpi` | Real per-capita disposable income in US dollars, and its percent growth rate |
| `Wages1` | `exper`, `school` | Years of work experience, and years of schooling |
| | `sex` | `male` or `female` |
| | `wage` | Hourly wage in 1980 dollars |
| `wage2` | `educ`, `wage` | Years of education, and monthly earnings |
| `finance-charts-apple.csv` | `Date`, `AAPL.Open`, ..., `AAPL.Adjusted` | Daily Apple share prices, plus four columns (`dn`, `mavg`, `up`, `direction`) derived before the file was published |
| `tylervigen.csv` | many | Unrelated time series, any two of which tend to correlate strongly |

A few features are worth knowing before you use these.

* `USArrests` stores state names as row names rather than as a column, which is why the book indexes with `USArrests[,'Murder']`.
* `USArrests` records *arrest* rates rather than offense rates, so differences across states reflect policing and reporting practice as well as crime.
* `state.region` lists states in the same order as `USArrests`, so you can attach it directly without a merge.
* Chapters 5--8 treat the 3294 workers in `Wages1` as the whole population, so sample statistics can be compared with a known truth.
  Chapters 5, 7, and 8 draw one random sample of 50 of these workers as their lab data.
  Chapters 18 and 19 do the same with `school` and `wage` stored in `population_xy`.
* With $n = 3294$, `Wages1` scatterplots need transparency to be readable, which is why [Figures](04_C_Figures.qmd) ties the alpha channel to sample size.

## Packages

R starts with `stats`, `graphics`, `grDevices`, `utils`, and `datasets` already loaded, which is where `lm()`, `plot()`, `rgb()`, `read.csv()`, and `USArrests` come from.
Every other package must be installed once and then loaded in each session, as explained in [First Steps](00_01_FirstSteps.qmd#packages).
[Code Conventions](04_B_CodeStyle.qmd) explains when to load a package with `library()`, when to call one function with `::`, and why datasets load with `data()`.

| Package | What the book uses it for | Chapters |
|---|---|---|
| `Ecdat` | The `Wages1` dataset | 2--3, 5--8, 10--25, 29 |
| `wooldridge` | The `wage2` dataset | 13, 29 |
| `mvtnorm` | Draws from a multivariate normal distribution, with `rmvnorm()` | 14, 18, 21 |
| `plotly` | Interactive figures, with `plot_ly()` | 20, 22, 26 |
| `reactable` | Interactive tables | 20 |
| `stargazer` | Formatted regression and summary tables | 20, 27--28 |
| `psych` | Scatterplot matrices, with `pairs.panels()` | 21 |
| `fixest` | Fixed-effects and instrumental-variable regressions, with `feols()` | 23, 27--28 |
| `sf` | Vector spatial data, such as county borders | 26 |
| `terra` | Raster spatial data, such as an elevation grid | 26 |
| `units` | Attaching units such as kilometers to distances | 26 |
| `knitr` | Placing images and tables on the page, in code the book hides | 1, 17, 20 |

```r
# Run once, in the console, not in your script
install.packages(c('Ecdat', 'wooldridge', 'mvtnorm', 'plotly', 'reactable',
    'stargazer', 'psych', 'fixest', 'sf', 'terra', 'units', 'knitr'))
```

On Linux, `sf` and `terra` also need the system libraries GDAL, GEOS, and PROJ.
Some chapters also name a package as a pointer to a ready-made version of something they build by hand, but you do not need these to run the book's code.
They are `spatstat.univar` for weighted quantiles (Chapter 3), `VGAM` for the Dagum distribution (10), and `DescTools` for Cramer's V (14).
Chapter 25 points to `strucchange` for the Chow test and `segmented` for an estimated break point.
Chapter 27 points to `ivreg` for instrumental-variable regression, and Appendix B points to `car` for variance inflation factors.

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Chapter 21 draws a scatterplot matrix with `psych::pairs.panels()`.
Restart R and run `pairs.panels(USArrests)` without the `psych::` prefix.
What happens, and what are two ways to fix it?

R reports that it cannot find the function `pairs.panels`, because `psych` is installed but not loaded.
Either write `psych::pairs.panels(USArrests)`, or run `library('psych')` once near the top of your script.
If R instead says there is no package called `psych`, then it is not installed, so run `install.packages('psych')` in the console first.
:::
